conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/name: Christian justifications of slavery and colonial wars
conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/reli: The Atlantic slave trade and the wars of colonial expansion were driven chiefly by profit, labour demand, state power and rivalry between European empires. Christianity contributed in two ways. First, papal bulls such as Dum diversas (1452) and Romanus pontifex (1455) extended the language of crusade against 'Saracens and pagans' to Africa, and theologians, preachers and planters used the conversion of Africans, the 'curse of Ham' and biblical passages regulating slavery to present enslavement and conquest as lawful and even benevolent. Second, churches and religious orders themselves owned plantations and enslaved people. Historians such as David Brion Davis argue that Christianity long accommodated slavery as part of the natural order, while also supplying the moral resources (Quaker conscience, evangelical revival, Catholic natural law, Black Christian prophecy) that eventually fuelled abolition; Willie James Jennings and others stress the role of Christian theology in forming modern ideas of race. Because religion legitimised rather than originated the trade, and Christians stood on both sides of the struggle, its role is best described as contributing.

conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/summ: From the Portuguese voyages of the fifteenth century to the abolition of slavery in Brazil in 1888, Christian authorities and thinkers repeatedly gave religious sanction to the enslavement of Africans and to wars against non-Christian peoples. Papal bulls authorised the 'perpetual servitude' of Africans, preachers taught that slavery brought heathens to salvation, and churches, religious orders and missionary societies owned enslaved people. Yet Christians were also among slavery's first and fiercest critics, and the movement that ended the Atlantic trade was led in large part by Quakers, evangelicals and enslaved Christians themselves.
conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/stor:
Slavery was accepted across the ancient and medieval Mediterranean, and Christian theology since Augustine had treated it as a consequence of sin rather than a natural right; medieval canonists allowed the enslavement of non-Christians captured in a just war. When Portuguese caravels reached West Africa, the chronicler Gomes Eanes de Zurara described the first large sale of Africans at Lagos in 1444 with pity but justified it by the captives' conversion. Pope Nicholas V's bull Dum diversas (1452) authorised King Afonso V to 'invade, search out, capture, vanquish and subdue all Saracens and pagans' and to reduce them to perpetual servitude, and Romanus pontifex (1455) confirmed Portugal's monopoly of the African coast. Alexander VI's Inter caetera (1493) divided newly found lands between Portugal and Spain on condition of evangelisation, the root of what was later called the 'doctrine of discovery'.

In the Spanish Americas the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos denounced the abuse of the Taíno in 1511, and the Requerimiento of 1513 required Indigenous peoples to accept the authority of the pope and the king on pain of war and enslavement. Bartolomé de las Casas fought the enslavement of Indigenous Americans, and the debate at Valladolid in 1550–51 pitted him against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, who invoked Aristotle's natural slavery. Las Casas had once proposed African labour as an alternative and later repented of it, but the Spanish and Portuguese crowns turned increasingly to enslaved Africans. In Kongo, whose Christian king Afonso I complained to Portugal in 1526 that traders were seizing his free subjects, and in Portuguese Angola, conquered in a series of wars from 1575, captives were commonly baptised en masse at Luanda before embarkation. Jesuits and other orders in Brazil and Spanish America owned plantations worked by enslaved people.

Protestant powers entered the trade in the seventeenth century and developed their own justifications. The 'curse of Ham' (Genesis 9) was widely read as condemning Africans to servitude; preachers cited the Old Testament laws on slavery and the apostolic instruction to slaves to obey their masters. Colonial wars against Native Americans were also framed providentially: after the destruction of the Pequot fort at Mystic in 1637, in which several hundred men, women and children died, the colonial commander John Mason presented the slaughter as God's own judgment on the 'heathen', and during King Philip's War (1675–76) Christian Indian converts were interned on Deer Island in Boston Harbour, where many died. France's Code Noir of 1685 required that enslaved people be baptised Catholic while codifying their status as property. The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, an Anglican mission society, inherited the Codrington plantations in Barbados in 1710 and worked them with enslaved people, branded with the word 'SOCIETY', until emancipation in 1834–38. George Whitefield campaigned to legalise slavery in Georgia and Jonathan Edwards owned enslaved people.

Christian opposition grew alongside. Capuchin missionaries Francisco José de Jaca and Epifanio de Moirans were imprisoned in Havana in 1681 for refusing absolution to slaveholders; the Afro-Brazilian Lourenço da Silva de Mendouça petitioned Rome against perpetual enslavement in 1684; and German and Dutch Quakers issued the Germantown protest in 1688. Quaker reformers such as Benjamin Lay, John Woolman and Anthony Benezet persuaded the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting to bar slave trading (1758) and slaveholding (1776). John Wesley's Thoughts upon Slavery (1774), the testimony of Olaudah Equiano and the evangelical Clapham circle around William Wilberforce helped secure the British abolition of the slave trade in 1807. Black Christians made the strongest case: Richard Allen founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and the Jamaican Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe led the 1831–32 rising that hastened British emancipation in 1833–34. Pope Gregory XVI condemned the slave trade in 1839.

In the United States, the conflict split the churches. Southern theologians such as Thornton Stringfellow and James Henley Thornwell defended slavery as biblical and divinely ordained, while Frederick Douglass contrasted 'the Christianity of Christ' with 'the slaveholding religion of this land'. The Methodists divided in 1844, the Southern Baptist Convention was formed in 1845 over the right of slaveholders to serve as missionaries, and the Presbyterians split in 1861; each side in the Civil War claimed God's favour. Nat Turner's 1831 revolt in Virginia was inspired by visions and biblical prophecy, and was crushed with bloody reprisals. Slavery ended with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, in Cuba in 1886 and in Brazil, the largest importer of enslaved Africans, in 1888.

As the Atlantic trade closed, the rhetoric of Christian civilisation was turned to colonial expansion in Africa. The General Act of the Berlin Conference (1884–85) pledged the powers to protect missionaries and suppress slavery while partitioning the continent, and Cardinal Charles Lavigerie launched an anti-slavery crusade in 1888 aimed at the East African and Saharan trade. King Leopold II's Congo Free State used humanitarian and Christian language while imposing forced labour that killed very large numbers of people; Protestant missionaries such as William Sheppard and Alice Seeley Harris later helped expose its atrocities. In recent decades churches have begun to acknowledge this history: the Southern Baptist Convention apologised in 1995, Georgetown University and the Jesuits acknowledged their sale of 272 enslaved people in 1838, the Church of England's Church Commissioners published research on their ties to the slave trade in 2023, and the Vatican formally repudiated the 'doctrine of discovery' in 2023.
conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/name: Papal bulls cast the subjugation of Africans as part of the crusade against Islam and paganism and as a means of saving souls. Portuguese and Spanish captives were baptised before shipment; the Requerimiento invoked God, the pope and the Spanish crown before war could be declared. Protestant planters and preachers cited the curse of Ham, Abraham's servants, the Mosaic slave laws and the Pauline command 'Slaves, obey your masters', and taught enslaved people a catechism of obedience. New England Puritans read victories over Native Americans as divine judgment on the 'heathen'. On the other side, abolitionists invoked the unity of humankind in Adam, the Golden Rule and the Exodus, and enslaved Christians sang of deliverance.

conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/casu: No total can be given for the colonial wars, and religious justification was only one factor among many. For the Atlantic slave trade, the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (Eltis and Richardson) estimates about 12.5 million Africans embarked between 1501 and 1866 and about 10.7 million landed, implying some 1.8 million deaths at sea; millions more died in capture, wars and marches in Africa and in the early years of plantation labour, but these deaths cannot be estimated precisely.
conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/effe: The forced migration of about 12.5 million Africans transformed the demography, economy and culture of the Americas and devastated many African societies.
Racial slavery created enduring patterns of racism and inequality in the Americas.
The 'doctrine of discovery' derived from papal bulls was cited in colonial and later national law, including the US Supreme Court's Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823), to dispossess Indigenous peoples.
Abolition movements, often religious in inspiration, became a model for later humanitarian and human rights campaigns.
Colonial partition of Africa from the 1880s was justified partly by the claim to suppress slavery and spread Christian civilisation.

Black Christianity, including independent churches such as the African Methodist Episcopal Church and the Black Baptist conventions, emerged from slavery and the rejection of segregated white churches.
American Methodists, Baptists and Presbyterians divided over slavery in 1844–61, divisions that shaped American Protestantism for a century or more.
Quakers, Methodists and evangelical Anglicans gained moral authority from their role in abolition.
Churches in Britain, the United States and Europe have since issued apologies and begun reparative projects for their ownership of enslaved people.
African and Caribbean Christians have developed theologies of liberation and reconciliation in response to this history.
conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/lega: The Christian justification of slavery and conquest is among the most painful chapters of church history, and it remains central to debates about race, reparations and the relationship between mission and empire. The same history shows Christian faith inspiring resistance and abolition, and today the descendants of enslaved Africans form a large part of global Christianity.

conflicts/slavery-and-colonial-wars/camp: Portuguese expansion down the African coast

Sanctioned by papal bulls, Portuguese ships established trading forts from Arguin to Elmina, a sugar colony on São Tomé, an alliance with Christian Kongo and finally the colony of Angola, which became the largest single source of enslaved Africans.
The triangular trade and the Middle Passage
British, French, Dutch and Portuguese slave ships

Ships carried manufactured goods to West Africa, exchanged them for captives who endured the Middle Passage to the Caribbean and North America, and returned with sugar, tobacco and cotton; Liverpool alone dispatched several thousand slaving voyages before 1807.
